title: What are they like?
goal: Describe people and things with adjectives that agree in gender and number, and put them in the right place.
bekal: forming feminine and plural adjectives, including the irregular ones
placing adjectives after the noun — except for a small group
wave: Review **Unit 9** first: say the birthdays of five people you know, then count from 70 to 99 without looking at the table.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Qui est-ce ?
dialogs.intro: Camille shows Budi a photo of her class, and he tries to guess who is who.

notes: **Adjectives agree with their noun in two ways: gender and number.** *Il est grand*, *elle est grande*, *ils sont grands*, *elles sont grandes*. English adjectives never change, so this has to become a new habit, not something you translate.

**The extra e often changes the sound.** *Grand* (GRAHN) → *grande* (GRAHND); *petit* (puh-TEE) → *petite* (puh-TEET). A consonant that was silent is now pronounced because an e follows it. That's how a French ear hears that the person is female.
**Adjectives come after the noun.** *Une fille sympathique*, *un livre intéressant*, *une voiture rouge*. This is the opposite of English — "a red car" becomes "a car red".

**Except for a small group that goes in front.** *Un **petit** garçon*, *une **grande** maison*, *un **vieux** monsieur*, *une **belle** ville*. The group is small and very common, so just memorize it: *beau, bon, grand, gros, jeune, joli, mauvais, nouveau, petit, vieux*.

**Aux cheveux courts** — the typical French pattern for physical features: *la fille **aux** cheveux courts*, *l'homme **aux** lunettes*. Literally "the girl with-the short hair". Note *à + les = aux*.
**Sympathique** (often shortened to *sympa*) means nice, friendly — not "sympathetic" in the sense of feeling sorry. It comes up in almost every French conversation about other people.
**Plus petit qu'elle** — comparisons use *que*, which becomes *qu'* before a vowel. The person compared takes the stressed form: *que **moi***, *que **toi***, *que **lui***, *que **elle***.

grammars.title: Forming feminine adjectives
body: There's really only one main rule: add **-e**. The rest are endings that change shape, plus a handful of words to memorize.
after: The truly irregular, common ones: *beau → belle*, *nouveau → nouvelle*, *vieux → vieille*, *long → longue*, *doux → douce*, *faux → fausse*, *gentil → gentille*, *frais → fraîche*.
Three of them have a special third form for masculine nouns before a vowel: *beau → **bel** homme*, *nouveau → **nouvel** an*, *vieux → **vieil** ami*. Purely for the sound.
Plurals: add a silent **-s**. The -eux ending doesn't change (*heureux → heureux*); the -al ending becomes -aux (*normal → normaux*).

grammars.title: Comparing
body: Three patterns cover everything you need at A1. The adjective still agrees with the person being compared.
after: ⚠️ *Bon* has its own comparative: *meilleur* (better), not *plus bon* — just like "better", not "gooder". For adverbs, *bien → mieux*. This is the mistake people notice fastest.
*Mauvais* can go either way: *plus mauvais* or *pire*. Both are correct.
After *que*, use the stressed forms: *moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles*. Not *je, tu, il*.

blocks.title: Describing faces and bodies
items: *Il est grand / petit / de taille moyenne.* — He is tall / short / of medium height.
*Elle a les cheveux longs / courts / blonds / bruns / noirs / roux.* — Her hair is long / short / blond / brown / black / red.
*Il a les yeux bleus / verts / marron.* — His eyes are blue / green / brown. ⚠️ *Marron* never changes form.
*Elle porte des lunettes.* — She wears glasses.
*Il a une barbe / une moustache.* — He has a beard / a mustache.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Hair and eye color use *avoir*, not *être*: *elle **a** les cheveux longs*, not *elle **est** cheveux longs*. Think "she has long hair", not "she is long hair".
